paper_title: Training Numerical Intelligence via Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of generating scientific code, but generating code is not the same as improving the algorithms behind it. For numerical solvers, execution feedback can expose poor performance, but rarely reveals its underlying cause and how to address it. We introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), a framework that links numerical diagnosis to reusable solver self-improvement. ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm that first explains why a solver performs poorly, then uses this diagnosis to guide the discovery of appropriate numerical methods. The resulting knowledge is packaged into reusable solver skills, turning solver improvement from trial-and-error editing into a structured process of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation. Across four challenging numerical domains--power flow equation, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ordinary differential equations, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs--ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. On GOC-500 power flow, for example, ADSD reduces mean solver error by nearly $71\times$, with improvements further transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly capable of writing scientific code and discovering algorithms (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). However, generating numerical solver is fundamentally different from building standard software. solver may run without errors and produce seemingly reasonable outputs, yet remain unnecessarily slow or fail on challenging instances due to numerical issues such as ill-conditioning, stiffness, or repeated matrix factorizations. Addressing these failures requires more than conventional debugging. An AI agent must understand why the solver behaves poorly, diagnose the underlying numerical condition, and select numerical method or modification tailored to that condition. This need for numerical diagnosis exposes major blind spot in todays scientific agents. Existing systems can generate or revise numerical code using execution traces and error feedback (Gaonkar et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026), search the literature for relevant techniques (Garikaparthi et al., 2025; Asai et al., 2026), and convert research papers into reusable tools (Gandhi et al., 2025; Miao et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026a). However, these capabilities are rarely coordinated. Execution feedback often leads to trial-and-error edits, while literature search relies on broad keywords. As result, an agent may detect poor solver performance without identifying its cause or the methods best suited to address it. This challenge is particularly notorious in numerical computing, where the same symptom can arise from different underlying causes. Since numerical methods also rely on specific assumptions and trade-offs, effective improvement requires first diagnosing the underlying numerical pathology and then identifying methods whose mechanisms and assumptions match it. Motivated by this gap, we argue that an effective numerical intelligence should explicitly separate three stages that current workflows often blur together: (i) observable behavior, which captures raw runtime evidence, such as residual histories and convergence logs; (ii) diagnostic knowledge, which interprets these observations by forming testable links between solver symptoms and their underlying numerical conditions; and (iii) executable solver knowledge, which finally translates 1 Preprint. Under review. the diagnosis into concrete numerical algorithms that are correctly implemented and packaged for direct integration into the solver. Building on this separation, we introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), automatic framework without updating model weights for numerical intelligence that operationalizes these stages through structured, diagnosis-first loop: solver behavior diagnose verified numerical condition retrieve targeted scientific knowledge implement executable solver skill We construct ADSD across four challenging classes of numerical problems: power flow equation solving, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ODE integration, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs, via three leading agent baselines, including GPT-5.5, Claude-sonnet-5, and Qwen3.8-2.4T. Moreover, our evaluations stress the numerical regimes with real-world engineering pressure, such as topology and feasibility shifts in power flow, near-loadability AC-OPF edge cases, stiff dynamical systems, and ill-conditioned high-contrast diffusion problems. Across these settings, ADSD consistently improves the solvers generated by the base models while preserving or improving computational efficiency. On power flow, for example, ADSD reduces Qwen3.8-2.4Ts mean error by 71 error reduction on GOC-500 power flow solver benchmark. Together, these results show that ADSD generates numerical knowledge that improves solver accuracy and efficiency across diverse scientific-computing tasks. Contributions. By introducing ADSD, we (i) provide practical and novel diagnosis-first paradigm for numerical intelligence, enabling agents to move systematically from solver behavior to verified numerical diagnoses and targeted numerical skills, and (ii) make ADSD as general framework for automated agent self-improvement, demonstrating consistent improvements across diverse numerical domains, language model families, and unseen problem regimes. Related works. Recent work advances numerical intelligence from algorithm discovery and simulation agents (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). In power engineering, the scale and complexity of real-world systems have led prior work to rely on multi-agent pipelines for solver construction and orchestration (Jia et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Shamseldein, 2026). Similar challenges arise in differential-equation solving for large dynamical systems. Prior work also studied whether LLMs can effectively use numerical solvers (Gaonkar et al., 2025), refine generated PDE solvers through execution feedback and debugging (Li et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026), and improve numerical reasoning through reinforcement learning (Cai et al., 2026). However, across both domains, existing methods provide limited mechanisms for transferring observed solver behavior to numerical deficiencies and acquiring relevant methods beyond its inherent knowledge, so general and efficient pipeline for training self-evolving numerical intelligence remains underexplored. Beyond numerical intelligence, Voyager (Wang et al., 2024) first demonstrated that embodied agents can acquire and reuse executable skills with the gradient-free paradigm. More recent work extends this idea to scientific settings by converting papers and other scientific resources into executable skills and workflows (Shen et al., 2026a; Gandhi et al., 2025; Miao et al., 2025), while using execution traces and validation feedback to guide skill discovery, refinement, and selection (Liu et al., 2026a; Moll et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026a). Complementary studies further investigate trajectory-based failure diagnosis and automated hypothesis falsification (Barke et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025a). Building on these directions, our work focuses specifically on diagnosis-guided acquisition of skills for numerical methods, and we defer discussions towards further related works to Appendix A.

sections.title: 3 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: We introduce the two core components of ADSD: auto-diagnosis and skill discovery. In practice, numerical agent must first understand why its solver struggles (i.e., diagnosis) before it can identify the right knowledge and tools to improve it. In our pipeline, auto-diagnosis identifies numerical conditions that explain solvers behavior, while skill discovery finds and builds re-usable empirical and theoretical methods from the literature. Together, they form diagnosis-driven pipeline that turns observed solver behavior into evidence-grounded solver improvements. Before running the pipeline, we partition the test cases into public and private sets. Feedback from the public cases is available for training and development, whereas the private cases remain hidden throughout the process and are reserved for final evaluation. literature database across power-grid and dynamic system solvers is also pre-constructed, serving as the specialized knowledge source for diagnosis and skill discovery. 3 Preprint. Under review.

sections.content: Our auto-diagnosis framework can be divided into the three key steps: (i) baseline solver generation, where we freeze baseline solver and collect its observable solving behavior on public testcases; (ii) diagnostic skill construction, where literature-grounded numerical knowledge is converted into executable diagnostic tests; and (iii) hypothesis verification, where the probes are used to identify and validate relationships between solver behavior and underlying numerical conditions. As shown in Algorithm 1, after data processing, the agent generates baseline solver N0 using its inherent knowledge and capabilities, with access to the public testcases for execution and debugging, as in standard coding-agent settings. Once finalized, N0 is frozen and rerun on all public testcases to record its observable behavior, including quantitative trajectories and summary statistics, which form the empirical basis for subsequent diagnosis. Throughout the full ADSD pipeline, the agent is prohibited from accessing off-the-shelf solvers, since our goal is to diagnose and improve the numerical capabilities already possessed by the base agent; off-the-shelf solver implementations would confound this comparison. Symptoms-condition diagnosis. The key here is to connect observable symptoms to the underlying numerical conditions that may cause them. Corresponding to lines 3-5 of Algorithm 1, we construct diagnostic skills via three steps. The agent first screens each paper using pre-processed preview containing its metadata, abstract, introduction, conclusion from the main text, retaining papers likely to contain concrete symptom-condition relationships. Shortlisted papers are then read in full, and each relationship is recorded as diagnostic claim with exact evidence, together with the observable quantities and running statistics from N0. Finally, claims sharing common diagnostic computation are grouped into diagnostic skills for next stage to generate and verify possible hypotheses. Hypothesis discovery. We use the resulting skill set to explain recurring solver behavior. First, we randomly seperate the public observations into non-overlapping diagnosis rounds {D1, . . . , Dn} and verification pool V, which checks the effectiveness of the hypotheses produced from each diagnosis round Di. Specifically, we perform diagnosis over multiple rounds to keep each round small enough for the agent to inspect individual traces and less frequent behaviors. For example, on IEEE-118, we split 5,000 public observations into 1,000 diagnosis cases across five rounds of 200 cases each, together with 4,000 verification cases. For each round i, the agent apply every skill in to the cases in Di. Using the diagnostic skills to examine each testcases input, solver trace, and final output, the agent then proposes hypotheses that connect observed solver symptoms to suspected numerical conditions. Each hypothesis is then converted into deterministic detector with explicit criteria for when the hypothesized relationship is considered supported or falsified. Each detector is then applied to V, and hypotheses that passed over 90% of are added to the verified set and marked as common illness, while rejected hypotheses are discarded. Finally, each verified hypothesis becomes targeted search guidance for skill discovery, and ADSD then finds the literature for methods that explain or address the common illness and converts sufficiently supported methods into executable solver skills to tackle such illness. 4 Preprint. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments consist of four main scanerios, together with additional results over further ablation analyses in 4.5. The four main experiments study power-flow equation solving (4.1), AC optimal power-flow control and optimization (4.2), ODE integration (4.3), and 2D diffusion PDE solving (4.4). Across all four benchmarks, we select recent datasets that represent challenging numerical tasks and closely reflect the practical difficulties faced by human engineers. 4.1 POWER FLOW (PF) EQUATION SOLVER Benchmark data. We apply training and evaluation cases from the IEEE and GOC grid families in PF (Rivera et al., 2025), which provides generalization settings along multiple dimensions. First, it includes multiple grid topologies: retains the full network, whereas N1 and N2 contain one and two fewer grid components, respectively. Moreover, it covers different operating regimes, including feasible (F) and close-to-infeasible (IF) cases. These regimes move progressively closer to the steady-state voltage-stability boundary and therefore become increasingly numerically challenging. Training & evaluation setup. We conduct training and evaluation on both the IEEE and GOC benchmark families. Because these families use different problem formulations and input-output schemas, solver developed for the IEEE setting cannot be directly applied to GOC. We consider three evaluation settings: (i) In-domain evaluation, which uses the same system configuration for 5 Preprint. Under review. Detailed results for figures (a) and (b) are presented in Tables 6 and 7, respectively. training and evaluation but evaluates on disjoint validation set; for example, the solver is trained on the IEEE-118 training set and evaluated on the same type of IEEE-118 validation set. (ii) Topology generalization, which evaluates the solver under different topology distribution; for example, the solver is trained on IEEE-118-N2 and evaluated on IEEE-118-N1. (iii) Feasibility generalization, which evaluates the solver under more harsh feasibility, e.g., the solver is trained on IEEE-118-F and evaluated on IEEE-118-IF. For the agent baselines, we select recent high-performing models that offer practical balance between agentic capability and inference cost, including closed-source model, GPT-5.5 and Claude-Sonnet-5, and one of strongest open-source models, Qwen3.8-2.4T. In-domain evaluation. We train the ADSD pipeline on the public test cases following the procedure in 3, and then evaluate the resulting solvers on hidden validation set drawn from the same grid topology and operating-regime difficulty. For example, the IEEE-118 benchmark contains 5,000 public cases and 10,000 hidden validation cases, with both sets using the N2 topology configuration and the feasible operating regime F. Table 1 reports solver wall-clock time and error on the IEEE-118 and GOC-500 validation sets. Across the evaluated base models, ADSD consistently improves solver performance, with the most significant gain observed for the Qwen3.8 baseline on GOC-500, where the agent reduces solver error by approximately 71 while maintaining comparable solver speed. These results indicate that ADSD can transform numerical patterns discovered from public cases into reusable solver skills that improve solution accuracy while preserving computational efficiency. Grid-topology generalization. We next examine whether solver skills learned exclusively from N2 topology cases can generalize without further adaptation to structurally more complete networks: N1 cases with one component removed and cases with the full grid intact. As shown in Figure 2(a), the skills learned from N2 generalize well across these unseen topologies, with significant improvement in solver performance across all base models and grid benchmarks. We note that this capability is particularly important in real power-grid applications, where engineers must routinely handle multiple network topologies, making it desirable for skills learned from one topology to remain reusable across different grid configurations. Grid-feasibility generalization. We further evaluate feasibility generalization by transferring skills learned exclusively from feasible cases (F) to substantially more challenging close-to-infeasible cases (IF). While feasible cases admit valid operating solutions, close-to-infeasible cases lie near at grid constraints, where ill-conditioning can make power-flow equations difficult to solve. This creates substantially more demanding setting that better reflects difficult scenarios encountered by power-system engineers. The corresponding results are shown in Figure 2(b). Unlike topology generalization, the room for improvement on close-to-infeasible cases is naturally more limited because the underlying grid constraints must be satisfied near the voltage-stability boundary. Nevertheless, even under these limitations, the learned skills still improve the infeasible-case solvers, demonstrating that the acquired numerical knowledge remains useful beyond the feasible training regime. sections.content: Different from the more recent PF benchmark, which focuses on solving power-system equations and evaluating generalization ability, OPFData (Lovett et al., 2024) targets classical power-system control and optimization. This extends our evaluation beyond solving AC power-flow equations to optimizing generation cost subject to the same physical equations and operational constraints. Such optimization becomes especially challenging as the system approaches its operating limits, motivating our evaluation on edge cases that resembles the realistic extreme real-world engineering difficulty. Edge-case design. Power-system operation becomes particularly challenging under high electricity demand, when operators must continue serving load at reasonable cost without violating grid operating limits. In these stressed regimes, generation and voltages are tightly coupled: adjusting generation at one location can alter network conditions elsewhere, so resolving one constraint may introduce another. Reliable optimization is therefore most critical near the systems operating boundary, where feasible margins are small and the solver must make effective decisions under severe network stress. Training & evaluation setup. To capture this realistic difficulty, among 300,000 cases from the IEEE-57 grid environment, we specifically filter 7,000 edge cases (2,000 for training and 5,000 for hidden evaluation) that operate near the maximum loadability of the system, with simultaneously high demand and transmission congestion. We evaluate solver quality using mean absolute relative objective error, fref/ max(fref, 1), where fref denotes the reference result from the benchmark, together with runtime and pass rate. Ablation analysis on ADSD. We first isolate the contribution of ADSDs discovered skills by removing the ADSD pipeline and directly asking each agent to improve its frozen baseline solver N0, without providing any diagnosed hypotheses or discovered skills. All remaining prompt instructions, model configurations, reasoning budgets, and runtime constraints are kept unchanged. We evaluate this ablation in two numerical domains: PF from power-grid engineering and stiff-ODE integration from dynamical-system engineering. 8 Preprint. Under review. Figure 3 compares the original N0 solver, direct self-improvement, and ADSD across three base models. Direct self-improvement produces inconsistent gains, which error decreases in four comparisons but increases in the remaining five. Still, ADSD achieves significantly lower error in all settings. These results indicate that simply requesting another solver revision does not reliably improve numerical performance, whereas the diagnostic hypotheses and literature-grounded skills discovered by ADSD provide substantially more consistent improvements across the evaluated models and domains. ADSD versus recursive self-improvement. The previous ablation considers only one round of direct self-improvement, raising the question of whether repeated revisions could eventually achieve comparable performance. We therefore extend the same procedure to five iterations, where at each iteration the agent can receive the solvers from all previous rounds. Shown in Figure 4, extending direct self-improvement to more iterations does not produce sustained error reduction. GPT baseline initially worsens, then partially recovers before plateauing above the error of its original N0 solver, while Claude-Sonnet-5 remains nearly unchanged across iterations. Thus, within the evaluated iteration budget, additional rounds of self-diagnosis and solver revision using inherent model knowledge alone do not close the performance gap to ADSD. Together with the single-round ablation, these results support the contribution of ADSDs externally discovered, diagnosis-targeted skills beyond simply allocating additional opportunities for solver revision.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In Appendix C, we provide more discussions and backgrounds for readers, along with further analysis of the necessity for agent to do diagnosis, which highlights that access to numerical knowledge alone does not determine which method addresses specific solver failure. We introduced ADSD, an automatic framework that turns observed solver behavior into verified numerical conditions and reusable executable skills. ADSD grounds solver improvement in literaturederived diagnostic probes, hypothesis verification, and final skill construction. Across four challenging numerical domains, ADSD improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency across different base models, with learned skills transferring to unseen problem regimes. Our ablations show that direct or recursive self-improvement using the models inherent knowledge does not recover these gains within the evaluated budgets. Together, these results highlight diagnosis as critical component of numerical intelligence, connecting observed solver behavior to actionable numerical knowledge. ADSD offers practical path toward scientific agents that identify why solver struggles, acquire appropriate methods, and retain them as reusable skills for improving the underlying numerical algorithms. 9 Preprint. sections.title: A FURTHER RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Power-system knowledge and applications. Foundation-model applications, domain-adapted models such as GAIA, and dispatch benchmarks, such as ElecBench, explore power-system knowledge and reasoning (Huang et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). Related studies enable LLMs to operate previously unseen simulation tools through documentation and prompting (Jia et al., 2024), or interpret observations for grid-fault diagnosis (Jing & Rahman, 2024). These tasks concern domain understanding, tool use, and physical-system conditions, while our work instead focuses on numerical conditions associated with solver behavior. Model discovery and formulation. An upstream problem is determining the mathematical model to be solved. SINDy identifies governing equations through sparse regression, while LLM-DMD uses language models to guide power-system dynamic model discovery (Brunton et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2026b). Other approaches translate natural-language requirements into optimization formulations and validate the generated models (Hu et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026c). Mamo (Huang et al., 2025b) similarly evaluates mathematical modeling for ODEs and optimization. For power models specifically, L2RPN (Marot et al., 2020) and RL2Grid (Marchesini et al., 2025) study reinforcement learning for sequential grid-operation decisions. Fan et al. (2022) and Biagioni et al. (2022) also provides the gym for training power agents. Numerical methods and solver evaluation. Classical numerical analysis provides the methods that solver-building agents can acquire. Newton power flow and higher-order methods with factorization reuse form relevant foundations (Tinney & Hart, 1967). Automated integrator design also predates LLMs: Guo et al. (2022) learn RungeKutta coefficients for targeted ODE families. For evaluation, Städter et al. (2021) compare integration methods and configurations on biological ODE models, while PETSc agent evaluation and PDEAgent-Bench assess generated scientific code for numerical accuracy, efficiency, and appropriate use of professional libraries (Zhang et al., 2026; Hang et al., 2026). We note that these studies emphasize that successful execution alone does not establish numerical quality. Scientific retrieval. We further discuss ADSDs scope to scientific retrieval literature. Recently, MIR (Garikaparthi et al., 2025) retrieves methodological inspirations, and OpenScholar (Asai et al., 2026) as well as PaperQA2 (Skarlinski et al., 2024) support literature-grounded scientific synthesis. The AI Scientist (Lu et al., 2024) and Agent Laboratory (Schmidgall et al., 2025) extend automation across literature review, experimentation, and research reporting. FlamePilot (Xiao et al., 2026) also connects literature with self-corrective combustion simulation workflows. For ADSD, it specializes this connection between literature and computation by checking numerical methods assumptions against an existing solver before constructing transferable implementation. We note that ADSD is complementary to these general skill-discovery frameworks. Paper2Agent (Miao et al., 2025) converts specified paper and its codebase into executable tools, SkillFoundry (Shen et al., 2026a) mines and validates skills from heterogeneous scientific resources, and Voyager (Wang et al., 2024) acquires reusable skills through execution feedback. Our skill-discovery stage (3.2) shares their goal of constructing reusable executable knowledge. ADSDs distinguishing focus is the preceding diagnostic step: it converts frozen solvers observed behavior into verified numerical hypotheses that specify which methods to retrieve and which assumptions their implementations must satisfy. This provides concrete connection between solver failures and skill acquisition, making existing skill-construction mechanisms complementary to the diagnosis front-end. Agentic skills aligned from experience. Finally, we go over prior classic works to incentive agents skill and ability. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) and ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) first turn execution feedback and accumulated experience into reusable guidance for subsequent tasks. Large Language Models as tool makers separates executable-tool construction from downstream tool use (Cai et al., 2024). Further works also studies reinforcement learning to improve the agents policy through skill, experience, and learning from mistakes (Wang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b), which establishes fundamental routes for retaining knowledge through memory, executable tools, and environment interactions (Guo et al., 2025). Apart from these in-context agentic tasks, recent LLM-RL framework also introduces also introduces language model to further incentive language models ability for mathematics (Li et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026c; Shao et al., 2024) and skill-based tool usage (Qian et al., 2025); We believe it is promising direction to extend ADSD to these domains as self-supervised pipeline as replacement the GPU-extensive online RL training. Lastly, language 14 Preprint. Under review. alignment methods (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; 2026d) also incurs online RL training, and how to adapt ADSD to the structure with contrastive signals and align language model would also be valuable direction to study.

sections.content: B.1 GPT BASELINE OVER PF We provide concrete walkthrough of the self-evolution process from 4.1 using the GPT baseline on the IEEE 118-bus training environment, which includes the initial N0 solver, the diagnosis skills learned, the initial symptoms identified together with the final verified hypotheses, the resulting skills built, and the final improved solver. Initial N0 solver. Before presenting the subsequent diagnosis and solver improvement, we first describe the baseline implementation produced by the agent. The resulting implementation is dense polar Newton power-flow solver with an analytic Jacobian, safeguarded step, and bounded regularized fallback for singular linear systems. Here is the core implementation of the N0 solver: for _ in range(MAX_ITERS): = jacobian(parsed, va, vm) dx = solve_linear_system(j, mismatch, diag) if dx is None: # one assembly # one factorization return failed_result(case_id, "jacobian solve failed", diag) base_scale = trust_region_scale(parsed, dx) accepted if accepted is None: = line_search(parsed, va, vm, norm, dx, base_scale) # 0.5 rad, 0.2 p.u. return failed_result(case_id, "line search failed", diag) va, vm, mismatch, norm, scale, step_norm = accepted diag["nonlinear_iterations"] += 1 if norm <= POWER_TOL: return success_result(parsed, va, vm, diag) Every accepted nonlinear iteration of N0 costs exactly one Jacobian assembly, one dense factorization, and one triangular solve. Therefore, for N0, one more Newton iteration and one more dense factorization are the same statement. This is what makes the diagnosis we next introduced actionable, and it is exactly the quantity that the two solver skills attack. Apart from the solver itself, N0 also records the following execution trace that the diagnosis stage utilizes for analysis: per-case counters for nonlinear iterations, Jacobian evaluations, factorizations, linear solves, fallback activations, and factorization failures, together with residual, step-norm, and accepted-step-scale histories. sections.title: C FURTHER DISCUSSIONS
sections.content: We report the detailed numerical statistics for the generalization experiments in 4.1. Tables 6 and 7 provide the complete results, including running times and standard deviations that are omitted from Figure 2. For literature-space construction, we directly collect papers from Google Scholar and the Semantic Scholar API using domain-level keywords (e.g., Newton power flow convergence and stiff ODE integration), resulting in the domain-specific literature database (e.g., 312 papers on PF equation solving and 376 papers on AC-OPF control). Taking PF as an example, weprovide some further discussions to help the general readers understand the impact of lower solver error from the perspective of professional power grid engineers. On the practical essence of solver residue. Specifically, it provides three practical impacts in realistic large-scale grids: (i) tighter residual control improves the numerical reliability of voltage and thermal-limit assessments following N1 or N2 contingencies. Near regular operating point, the error in monitored quantity satisfies the first-order relation δg gJ 1r, where is the power-flow Jacobian and is the residual; smaller residual therefore improves the corresponding sensitivityweighted error bound, enabling more reliable assessment of small security margins (Higham, 2002). Second, lower residuals help distinguish small changes caused by redispatch, reactive-power support, or transformer adjustments from numerical solution errors. This is particularly valuable for finitedifference sensitivity calculations, in which errors from individual power-flow solutions are amplified by the inverse perturbation size (Moré & Wild, 2012). Third, tighter power-balance satisfaction provides more consistent equilibrium initial conditions for dynamic simulations, reducing the potential for artificial transients caused by initialization mismatches (Molzahn & Lesieutre, 2013). These benefits make residual control relevant beyond binary convergence test, particularly under stressed or ill-conditioned operating conditions (Canizares & Alvarado, 1993); the required accuracy should be determined by downstream sensitivities and decision margins. On the role of diagnosis. Effective solver improvement requires connecting observed failures to the numerical methods capable of addressing them. Our case studies illustrate why diagnosis is therefore essential, and why simply exposing an agent directly to broad literature space and asking it to improve the solver is often ineffective. In Appendix B.2, the baseline already implements primaldual interior-point method, but omits the specific scaling and progress-measure mechanisms needed to resolve its stalling behavior. Diagnosis converts this observed failure into targeted search for row scaling and normalized KKT progress measures from Wächter & Biegler (2006), well-established techniques underlying Ipopt and described in classic work that should be already represented in the training data of frontier models. This suggests that access to numerical knowledge itself is not the primary barrier; rather, the central challenge is identifying which knowledge is relevant to the failure at hand and retrieving it accordingly. 19 Preprint. Under review. In Appendix B.1, diagnosis similarly identifies progress per Jacobian factorization as the relevant search objective, narrowing 312 papers to 82 candidates and ultimately six papers for full-text examination. Separately, the five-round GOC-500 experiment shows that repeated solver revisions alone do not close the gap to ADSD. Together, these observations support diagnosis as the mechanism that makes existing numerical knowledge actionable: it determines which methods to seek, explains why they are appropriate for the observed failure, and specifies the properties that their implementation must preserve.
